old: She went back into the house wondering and took her son’s words to heart.
new: She went back into the house in wonder, and kept her son’s words in her heart.
reason: Butler: “She went wondering back into the house, and laid her son’s saying in her heart” — the identical Butler sentence is fixed at accepted B01-P026 as “kept her son’s words in her heart” (GLOSSARY formula row: “taking … to heart” means accepting or being wounded, not pondering); the draft reinstates the exact rendering that row was written to remove.

old: Then she went with her servants to the storeroom
new: Then she went with her maids to the storeroom
reason: Butler: “she then went with her maidens into the store-room” — accepted B18-P20 and B19-P38 render Butler’s “maidens” as “maids”; “servants” generalizes and merges it with Butler’s separate word “servants” (¶21, ¶24).
Butler: “Along with her came her maidens” — same as ¶0 (accepted B18-P20, B19-P38: “maids”).

new: when he hands the wine around
reason: Butler: “from the place at which the cupbearer begins when he is handing round the wine” — the order of turns follows the cupbearer’s circuit; “pours” drops the going-round the direction rule depends on.

new: He was the suitors’ sacrificial priest
reason: Butler: “He was sacrificial priest to the suitors” — qualifier dropped.

old: for his hands were soft and unused
new: for his hands were weak and unused
reason: Butler: “for his hands were weak and unused to hard work” — D29, Butler’s own word; “soft” is a different quality.

old: Some of us are even now hoping and praying to marry Penelope, but when he has seen
new: Someone among us is even now hoping and praying to marry Penelope, but when he has seen
reason: Butler: “Some one of us is even now hoping … but when he has seen this bow” — the plural leaves the following “he … him” without an antecedent for a listener.
Butler: “a large ball of lard” — concrete noun generalized (Voice and form: concrete nouns kept); “lard” is current English.
Butler: “a great ball of lard” — same as ¶13, keeps the repetition.

old: Let this be our signal: the suitors
new: Let this also be our signal; the suitors
reason: Butler: “let this moreover be the token between us; the suitors will …” — PUNCTUATION §6 allows an added colon only to introduce a list; restore Butler’s semicolon and his “moreover”.
Butler: “among the Lapithae” — not a Roman name in the closed table, so it stays as Butler spells it (ODY-RULES: already-Greek names unchanged).

new: string the mighty bow of Odysseus
reason: Butler: “string the mighty bow of Ulysses” — the epithet belongs to the bow, as in ¶2 (“the mighty bow of Odysseus”), not to the man.
Butler: “your own boarhounds” — concrete noun generalized; “boarhound” is current English and the dogs Eumaeus keeps for boar are the point of the taunt.

old: for I’m the stronger man of the two
new: for I’m the better man of the two
reason: Butler: “for I am the better man of the two. I wish I was as much stronger …” — Butler’s two words (better / stronger) are collapsed into one.

old: for when he went to the house of Zeus’s son, mighty Heracles, who performed such incredible feats of valor, Heracles shamefully killed him, though he was his guest
new: for when he went to the house of Zeus’s son, mighty Heracles, who performed such incredible feats of valor, Heracles shamefully killed him, though Iphitus was his guest
reason: 'he was his guest' stacks two pronouns right after two named men (Iphitus, Heracles) in the same breath; a listener has to work out which 'he' is the guest and which 'his' is the host. Naming Iphitus resolves it instantly without adding new information.

old: I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am than you
new: I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am stronger than you
reason: The elliptical double comparative ('as much stronger... as I am than you') drops the second 'stronger,' which is easy to follow silently on the page but hard to parse by ear — the listener has to mentally supply the missing word. Restoring it keeps the same meaning and rhythm while removing the ambiguity.

old: He took an arrow that was lying on the table—for those which the Achaeans would soon taste were all inside the quiver—and laid it on the center grip of the bow.
new: He took an arrow that was lying on the table and laid it on the center grip of the bow; the rest, which the Achaeans would soon taste, were all inside the quiver.
reason: This is the exact moment the listener needs to picture cleanly: Odysseus reaching for the arrow he's about to shoot through the axes. The aside interrupts that single action with a euphemism ('would soon taste') and a name ('the Achaeans') that, in every earlier book, has meant the army at Troy — here it means the suitors in the room. A first-time listener is likely to lose the thread of 'he took an arrow... and laid it' while puzzling over who is tasting what. Swapping in 'the suitors' and 'would soon feel' keeps the foreshadowing but removes the two things most likely to stall a listener at the one moment that most needs to stay vivid. [lead: keeps Butler’s “Achaeans” and “taste” (name rule; no substitution); the action now reads as one continuous movement, the aside follows it]
